source.title: Surrogate Fidelity: When Can Open LLMs Explain Closed Ones?
source.authors: Philippe Chlenski; Zachariah Carmichael; Ayush Warikoo; Chia-Tse Shao; Yingxiao Ye; Ao-Bo Yang; Vivek Miglani; Nehal Bandi

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper and appendices; no truncation or garbling that prevents extraction is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares cross-model prediction, ablation-attribution, and representation-level agreement. Its results qualify convergence: some signals agree strongly, while attribution-relevant alignment is much lower; outcomes also vary by metric, benchmark, granularity, confidence, and prompt condition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own cross-model agreement measurements and interventions, so these are in scope. Rows below use aggregates where the paper reports aggregates over model pairs; no individual-pair values have been inferred. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures cross-model agreement across 11 LLMs (Qwen, Llama, GPT, Gemini). Signals include log-odds (a readout projection of representations), perturbation norm and readout alignment (Fmag, Falign), and attribution projections, plus a CKA comparison. Agreement is far from complete in the readout direction and depends strongly on the measure, granularity, benchmark, confidence, layer and prompt. The authors argue the Platonic 'Forms' fan out (low Falign) while appearances converge (high Fpred). This bears on V6 and V7. It does not measure a scale trend in cross-architecture alignment, so V1 is not tested as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that neither prediction- nor representation-level fidelity (attention, perturbation magnitude, CKA) implies attribution fidelity. Models agree on outputs but diverge in readout directions. They frame this against the Platonic hypothesis as appearances converging while 'Forms' fan out. Surrogate validity should be measured at the level of the explanation, not assumed.
record.recipe_differences: Uses cross-model prediction, leave-one-out attribution, perturbation-response, attention, and CKA comparisons; it does not reproduce either original source's specific method. It is a direct study of cross-model agreement in language models, not a direct scale law or multimodal convergence experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Agreement varies with benchmark and scoring method, sentence- versus word-level ablation, confidence quintile, relative layer depth, attention aggregation method, and system-prompt condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention importance scores agree highly across models (mean Fattn median .905, rollout .848, max .855) and are flat across confidence bins (.958).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention patterns over input segments are highly consistent across LLMs of different families and sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: White-box signals from one model barely predict another model's ablation attributions (Fmag→attr median .074, attention→attr ≤.004).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal signals of an open surrogate poorly predict a target model's causal input attributions.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimized system prompts transfer poorly across models (mean Δaccuracy −1.4%), and models differ in susceptibility to being shifted toward a donor model (VT from −0.09 to +0.71).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-level behavioural convergence across models is directional and model-specific.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, 2026
record.problems: The evaluation focuses mainly on binary classification and leave-one-out input ablation; the authors note that ablations may shift inputs off-distribution and that this intervention trades mechanistic depth for API compatibility. Closed models lack internal measurements, representation-level analyses are limited to open models, some appendix results are figure-only, and the study does not establish a general scale trend or test other modalities.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Figure-only scale plots of Qwen log-odds separation were not recorded as cross-model alignment results because they do not directly measure similarity between models.

untested.parts: Whether cross-architecture alignment rises with size or capability. Only aggregates are recorded; the per-pair data are within one family and mixed across families (see missing).
All; no vision-language or paired image-caption data.
No learned map, stitching, relative or unpaired transfer. The paper only argues that low r² rules out a readout-compatible linear map.
All; no neuron, SAE-feature or circuit matching.

Plateau, and whether shared data or objectives cause the alignment. Instruction tuning drives log-odds separation (Fig 7), but no cross-model alignment comparison of base against instruct models is reported.

missing.what: Per-pair Falign and Fmag within Qwen by size (e.g. Falign 0.5B–3B .110, 3B–7B .262, 7B–14B .294) and Llama-8B against Qwen sizes. Bears on a scale trend.
Per-pair Fpred and Fattr heatmap: Qwen-0.5B outlier (Fpred ~.09–.18 with other Qwen models) against Qwen-7B/14B .796; within-family above cross-family (max cross-family .684).
Instruct vs base Qwen log-odds separation across 0.5B–32B. Base models stay near zero; separation is attributed to instruction tuning.
Falign by benchmark (BoolQ .200, ANLI .060–.078, WinoGrande .018, LAMBADA .024).
RV of random and unembedding projections converging toward full CKA; unembedding projections plateau lower.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 labels were dropped. The recorded rows are all-pair aggregates and cannot show convergence with scale; r17 was not even linked to V1. The study's relevance to the claim is mainly V6 (strong measure and input dependence) and V7 (incomplete alignment in the readout direction). Fpred and Fattr are 1-d projections of representations and perturbations, not full representational similarity. The authors note the Platonic paper uses nearest-neighbour measures, which they did not test. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish a general monotonic relationship between model size or capability and geometric similarity across architectures, objectives, data, or modalities. The scale analysis of Qwen log-odds separation is not a direct test of cross-model distance convergence.
No paired image-caption data or vision-language model comparison.
No comparison of independent training seeds or shared feature subspaces across seeds.

The paper discusses readout-compatible linear transfer and measures agreement between scalar readouts and CKA, but does not report an actual learned representation map, model stitching, relative-representation transfer, or unpaired mapping result.
No test of recurring interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits across models.
The tested variations include benchmarks, ablation granularity, confidence bins, attention aggregation, layer depth, and system-prompt conditions. No out-of-distribution test is reported.

The study shows incomplete agreement and differences associated with instruction tuning, but does not establish that shared training data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, cause alignment.
